newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Tame Feb CPI rise won't avert Fed hike.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Tame Feb CPI rise won't avert Fed hike.

text.p: U.S. consumer prices probably remained well behaved in February but that should not stop the Federal Reserve from executing a preemptive interest rate hike next week, economists said.

The February consumer price index (CPI), due Wednesday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT is expected on average to have advanced a moderate 0.2 percent after a 0.1 percent increase in January, according to a poll of U.S. economists.

"Market participants may take comfort from it but the question is: 'Will the Fed?' My answer to that is if the Fed were going to wait for retail inflation to pick up, then the horse would be well out of the barn," said Dick Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.

Last week's sharp 0.4 percent fall in February producer prices may not be a perfect leading indicator for CPI this week, economists said. They said they were not lulled into forecasting quiescent wholesale prices would sway the Fed from tightening credit at its next policy-setting meeting.

The Federal Open Market Commitee meets to consider interest rates on March 25. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has recently said he might raise interest rates to slow the economy even though there are few solid sign of inflation.

"We had a chorus of views that are identical to that from other Fed officials saying you can not wait if you're a central banker for (inflation) to occur and they are looking for advanced indicators of inflation.
"Signals on that score have been mixed but nevertheless have been tilting towards higher inflation," Berner said.

Energy prices at the retail level are likely to be contained, as last year's blip higher continues to dissipate, economists said. But CPI is unlikely to mimic the 1.2 percent decline in February energy prices reflected in last week's producer price index, forecasters said.
When food and energy prices are subtracted, economists surveyed by Reuters expect consumer prices also rose just 0.1 percent matching the previous month's benign increase.
The Labor Department uses a different series for measuring food and energy prices in CPI it does in PPI, said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures.
Tainer's CPI forecasts match the survey consensus.
"Even though we did see that sharp drop in energy prices in PPI were not going to see the same thing on CPI," she said.
On the other hand, higher wholesale food prices might spill over somewhat into the CPI data, economists said.
Coffee prices were up sharply in February and a freeze boosted wholesale vegetable prices, said Mike Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.

"Right now we're benefitting by the reversal of the energy blip up late last year and that is probably holding down the overall number somewhat," Niemira said. "But it's a constant rotation by commodity, without much real change in pace.
"Overall, I would say the CPI news is very favorable, but I don't think it is going to matter much with respect to the Fed," Tainer said.
